Drawing on principles of self-determination, just war theory, and historical precedent, it posits that the aggressor's initiation of force creates a reciprocal ethical obligation for the oppressed to defend themselves, thereby restoring justice and humanity.

The Ethical Foundation: Self-Determination as an Inalienable Right

At the core of the argument for violent resistance lies the universal principle of self-determination, enshrined in Article 1 of the United Nations Charter (1945), which declares that "all peoples have the right of self-determination." This is not a mere diplomatic platitude but a profound ethical axiom rooted in the dignity of the human person. Philosopher John Locke, in his Second Treatise of Government (1689), articulated the natural right to life, liberty, and property, arguing that when a tyrant or invader encroaches upon these, the people may rightfully revolt. In colonial contexts, occupation is the ultimate violation of this triad: land is seized, liberties are curtailed, and lives are devalued or extinguished.

Ethically, non-violent resistance, while admirable, often proves insufficient against entrenched colonial powers that respond to peaceful demands with brute force. Mahatma Gandhi's satyagraha in India succeeded partly because Britain faced global scrutiny post-World War II; however, in isolated or heavily militarized occupations, such as the Algerian struggle against French rule (1954–1962), non-violence was met with massacres, torture, and internment. The National Liberation Front's (FLN) armed uprising, though brutal, ultimately compelled France's withdrawal, leading to independence. To deny colonized peoples the right to violence in such scenarios is to impose a moral asymmetry: the colonizer wields lethal force unapologetically, while the colonized must remain passive, perpetuating their subjugation. As Frantz Fanon argues in The Wretched of the Earth (1961), violence is a "cleansing force" that humanizes the oppressed, breaking the psychological chains of inferiority imposed by colonialism.

Just War Theory and the Proportionality of Resistance

Just war theory, developed by thinkers like St. Augustine and Thomas Aquinas, provides a robust ethical framework for evaluating violent resistance. It distinguishes between jus ad bellum (the justice of resorting to war) and jus in bello (justice in the conduct of war). For colonized peoples, the criteria for jus ad bellum—just cause, right intention, last resort, and proportionality—are readily met. The "just cause" is self-defense against an aggressor who has initiated and sustained violence; the "right intention" is liberation, not conquest; the "last resort" is invoked after diplomatic and non-violent avenues fail, as seen in the Palestinian intifadas; and proportionality weighs the harm of occupation (genocide, displacement, cultural erasure) against the resistance's aims.

Consider the Native American resistance to European settler colonialism in the 19th century. Treaties were routinely violated, and genocidal campaigns like the Trail of Tears (1830s) displaced entire nations. Warriors such as those in the Sioux Wars or the Apache under Geronimo employed guerrilla tactics not out of bloodlust but necessity, defending homelands against an existential threat. Ethically, this resistance was proportional: the colonizers' industrialized warfare and scorched-earth policies dwarfed indigenous responses, which were defensive and localized. International law echoes this, with the Geneva Conventions (1949) recognizing the right of occupied peoples to resist, provided it adheres to humanitarian standards. The 1977 Additional Protocol I explicitly protects "armed conflicts in which peoples are fighting against colonial domination" as legitimate struggles for self-determination.

Moreover, the moral calculus shifts when occupation is framed as ongoing aggression. As Hannah Arendt notes in On Revolution (1963), revolutions born of oppression are ethically superior to the status quo, for they seek to end injustice rather than perpetuate it. Violent resistance, when targeted at military occupiers rather than civilians, aligns with this ethic, mirroring the Allied use of force against Nazi occupation in World War II—a precedent without which the world might still languish under fascist rule.

Historical Precedents and the Limits of Pacifism

History abounds with examples where violent resistance dismantled colonial yokes, underscoring its ethical validity. The Haitian Revolution (1791–1804), led by enslaved Africans against French planters, was the first successful slave revolt in the Americas. Facing extermination, the revolutionaries under Toussaint Louverture employed decisive violence, establishing the world's first Black republic. Without it, the ethical horror of chattel slavery would have endured unchallenged. Similarly, in Vietnam, Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh forces resisted French and American imperialism through protracted warfare, culminating in independence and unification. These victories were not moral aberrations but fulfillments of ethical duty: to prioritize collective liberation over individual pacifism when the latter enables atrocity.

Critics of violent resistance often invoke absolute pacifism, citing figures like Martin Luther King Jr., who championed non-violence in the U.S. civil rights movement. Yet King's success relied on a democratic framework and media amplification unavailable to most colonized peoples. In occupied territories like Palestine or Kashmir, where checkpoints, settlements, and blockades render daily life a form of slow violence, non-violence can become complicity in one's own erasure. As Malcolm X powerfully stated, "If you're not ready to die for [freedom], then you don't deserve to live." Ethically, this underscores that the right to self-defense extends to lethal means when life itself is at stake—a principle affirmed in every legal system's recognition of homicide in self-defense.

Counterarguments that label resistance as "terrorism" ignore the colonizer's monopoly on violence. Edward Said, in Orientalism (1978), critiques how Western narratives dehumanize resistance to maintain imperial legitimacy. Morally, the true terrorism is the structural violence of occupation: apartheid walls, resource extraction, and demographic engineering that render indigenous existence untenable. Violent resistance, as a response, restores ethical balance, compelling accountability from powers insulated by military might.

Conclusion

The right of colonized peoples to violent resistance is not a call to anarchy but a profound ethical affirmation of human agency against dehumanization. Grounded in self-determination, just war principles, and historical necessity, it recognizes that peace imposed by subjugation is no peace at all. By any means necessary, as Malcolm X urged, the oppressed must reclaim their sovereignty, for in doing so, they not only defend their bodies and lands but reaffirm the moral arc of the universe toward justice. To withhold this right is to endorse the very colonialism that scars our shared history. In an era of lingering occupations, acknowledging this imperative is the first step toward genuine global equity.

The moral weight of this right is further reinforced by the international legal framework regarding self-determination. This principle implies that no people should be forced to live under the political domination of another without their consent. When peaceful avenues for decolonization—such as negotiation, diplomacy, or legal recourse—are blocked by the occupying power, the right to self-determination transforms into a right to active liberation. If the colonizer refuses to acknowledge the political agency of the occupied, the occupied must reclaim that agency. When an occupying power views the resistance of the colonized as "terrorism" while their own actions constitute "law and order," the moral high ground is illusory. In such scenarios, where dialogue is impossible and peaceful protest is met with lethal force, violent resistance becomes the only remaining language the oppressor understands. The alternative to violent resistance is not peace; it is the continuation of theft, cultural erasure, and the denial of basic human rights. Moreover, the "cycle of violence" is initiated by the colonizer. The colonized are merely breaking that cycle through the assertion of their sovereignty.

When peaceful means are rendered impossible by the nature of the occupation, the use of force becomes a tragic but necessary tool for liberation. The Moral Imperative of Self-Defense

One of the most fundamental moral principles is the right to self-defense. This principle is universally recognized and is enshrined in various legal and ethical frameworks. When a people are subjected to foreign occupation, their fundamental rights, including the right to life, liberty, and security, are violated on a massive scale. In such circumstances, the use of violence to defend oneself and one's community becomes a moral imperative. Colonized peoples are not merely defending their physical existence but also their cultural, social, and economic integrity.

The Ethical Justification of Resistance

Ethical theories, particularly those rooted in deontological and consequentialist frameworks, provide additional justification for violent resistance. Deontological theories, which emphasize the inherent moral worth of actions, argue that certain actions are right or wrong in and of themselves, regardless of their consequences. In the context of colonial resistance, the use of violence to resist oppression can be seen as a moral duty to uphold justice and human dignity. Conversely, consequentialist theories, which evaluate actions based on their outcomes, suggest that if violent resistance leads to the liberation and empowerment of colonized peoples, it is ethically justified.

Historical Precedent and International Law

Historical examples and international law also support the right to violent resistance. The right of colonized peoples to resist occupation is a foundational principle of international law and human rights. The ethical justification for such resistance is rooted in the inherent right to self-determination and the necessity of defending against oppression. While violence is a complex and tragic aspect of conflict, history and legal theory provide a robust framework for understanding why colonized people may legitimately resort to armed struggle as a last resort.

The Context of Structural Violence

To understand the morality of resistance, one must first recognize the nature of colonization itself. Colonization is not merely a political arrangement; it is a system of structural violence. It involves the displacement of indigenous populations, the theft of resources, the destruction of culture, and the imposition of foreign rule through force. When a people are colonized, they are subjected to a continuous state of violence—whether through economic exploitation, police brutality, or military occupation.

In this context, the "peace" often touted by colonizers is merely the silence of subjugation. As Frantz Fanon argued in The Wretched of the Earth, colonialism is not a thinking machine, nor a body endowed with reasoning faculties. It is violence in its natural state, and it will only yield when confronted with greater violence. Therefore, the violence of the colonized is not the initiation of conflict but a reaction to an existing, pervasive state of oppression.

International Legal Frameworks

The right to resist is codified in international law, specifically within the framework of self-determination. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Article 3) states that everyone has the right to life, liberty, and security of person. When a colonial power denies a people their self-determination and subjects them to military occupation, they strip away these fundamental liberties.

Furthermore, the right to resist occupation is enshrined in the Geneva Conventions and additional protocols, which recognize the legitimacy of struggles against colonial domination and alien occupation. Protocol I explicitly affirms the right of peoples to self-determination and provides legal protections for combatants engaged in such struggles, provided they adhere to the laws of war. This legal recognition acknowledges that when peaceful avenues for self-determination are blocked by an occupying force, armed resistance becomes a legitimate extension of the right to exist as a free people.

The Moral Imperative of Self-Defense

Ethically, the right to violent resistance is grounded in the universal principle of self-defense. If an individual has the right to defend themselves against a lethal attack, a collective people possess the same right against existential threats. Colonization often threatens not just the present existence of a people but their future survival. When a colonizing power destroys the environment, erases cultural identity, and disenfranchises a population, the threat is not only physical but existential.

Pacifism is a noble moral stance, but it is a privilege often afforded to those who are not facing immediate annihilation. To demand non-violence from a people suffering under the boot of military occupation is to demand complicity in their own erasure. When all diplomatic channels are sealed and peaceful protests are met with bullets, the state has effectively removed the social contract, leaving the people with no alternative but to defend themselves.

The Ethics of Proportionality and Discrimination

While the right to resistance is morally justified, the ethics of how that resistance is conducted remain subject to the principles of proportionality and discrimination. However, these principles must be viewed through the lens of asymmetry. An occupied people rarely possess the military capacity to engage a colonial power on equal footing. Their resistance often takes the form of guerilla warfare, which, while asymmetrical, is a tactical response to an overwhelming imbalance of power.

The moral burden of violence ultimately rests with the oppressor, who initiates the conditions of war. The violence of the colonizer is violence to maintain an unjust status quo; the violence of the colonized is violence to restore justice and freedom. As Martin Luther King Jr. noted, "Violence is the language of the unheard." When a system is designed to suppress a people, the destruction of that system—though violent—is a moral necessity to achieve a higher peace.

The right of colonized people to use violent resistance is not a call for chaos, but a desperate assertion of humanity against dehumanization. It is a response to the entrenched violence of occupation and a tool for reclaiming the right to self-determination. While the ideal path is always one of peaceful negotiation, history has shown that oppressive regimes rarely relinquish power without pressure. Ethically and legally, when a people are denied their right to exist freely, they retain the inherent right to defend themselves by any means necessary. True peace cannot exist without justice, and justice cannot exist without the freedom of the colonized to determine their own destiny.

The Moral Case for Resistance to Colonization—And the Ethical Limits on Force

Colonization and military occupation are not merely political arrangements; they are systems that typically involve coercion, dispossession, and the denial of a people’s ability to govern themselves. When a population is ruled without consent—often through force, legal inequality, and restrictions on movement, speech, and economic life—resistance is not simply predictable; it can be morally intelligible. The core ethical claim is straightforward: human beings and communities have a right to freedom, dignity, and collective self-determination, and persistent domination can create a moral permission—sometimes even a moral duty—to resist.

1) Self-determination as a foundational moral right

At the heart of anti-colonial ethics is the principle that a people are not property. They are not raw material to be administered for another’s benefit, nor a “problem” to be managed indefinitely. Self-determination is both an individual and collective moral interest: individuals need meaningful control over the conditions of their lives, and communities need political agency to preserve culture, security, and the material basis of survival. Colonization, by design, frustrates these ends.

From a deontological perspective (focused on rights and duties), colonization violates the basic duty to treat persons as ends in themselves. If a population is governed through coercion and denied equal political standing, they are being treated instrumentally—valued for land, labor, strategic advantage, or ideological prestige. Under such conditions, resistance can be understood as an assertion of moral equality.

2) Oppression, coercion, and the moral logic of self-defense

Many moral traditions recognize self-defense as a justification for the use of force in narrow circumstances: when an aggressor threatens life or imposes severe rights-violations, and when nonviolent alternatives are unavailable or have been systematically foreclosed. In contexts where occupation involves routine violence, arbitrary detention, collective punishment, or enforced displacement, the claim that the dominated have no right to defend themselves risks becoming an insistence that they must accept ongoing harm as their permanent condition.

That said, the ethical logic of self-defense is not a blank check. Even when the cause is just, the means must remain constrained by principles that protect human life and reduce suffering.

3) Just war ethics: just cause does not mean any means

Just war theory—often invoked in debates about resistance—helps clarify why the legitimacy of a political goal does not automatically legitimate every tactic. It typically requires:

  • Just cause (e.g., resisting aggression, defending basic rights)
  • Last resort (force only when peaceful remedies are genuinely unavailable)
  • Proportionality (harms inflicted must not outweigh the good sought)
  • Discrimination/noncombatant immunity (civilians must not be targeted)

Anti-colonial resistance may satisfy “just cause” when it aims to end domination and defend fundamental rights. But it fails morally when it abandons discrimination and proportionality—especially when civilians are treated as tools for signaling, retaliation, or leverage. Ethical resistance cannot be grounded in the same dehumanization that makes colonization wrong in the first place.

4) International law: a recognized right to self-determination, strict limits on violence

Modern international norms widely affirm self-determination and prohibit conquest and apartheid-like domination. At the same time, international humanitarian law is emphatic that civilians may not be targeted, regardless of grievances or political aims. The law’s premise is morally important: even in war, some acts are forbidden because human dignity does not disappear under oppression or desperation.

This framework does not require the oppressed to be passive, but it does insist that the struggle for liberation must not be waged by erasing the moral status of uninvolved people. The strongest moral argument against colonization is that every person counts; violating that principle undermines the very foundation of liberation.

5) The ethical center of resistance: restoring dignity without reproducing domination

One reason violent rhetoric can be seductive in occupied societies is that it expresses rage at humiliation and powerlessness. Yet a liberation ethic is ultimately judged not only by what it overthrows, but by what it builds. Resistance aimed at freedom must discipline itself around a vision of equal human worth—otherwise it risks becoming another project of domination with different beneficiaries.

This does not deny the tragedy of situations where force seems unavoidable. It insists, rather, that the moral burden of an occupying power’s coercion does not erase the moral constraints on everyone else. The ethical task is to resist injustice while refusing the logic that “anything goes.”

Conclusion

Colonization and occupation are profound moral wrongs that violate self-determination and human dignity. People living under such conditions have strong moral and legal grounds to resist and to seek freedom, including through forms of defense recognized by ethical and legal tradition. But the most compelling justification for resistance is inseparable from moral limits: proportionality, last resort, and—above all—the protection of civilians. A struggle for liberation is at its most ethically coherent when it seeks to end domination without replicating the devaluation of human life that made domination possible.

  • Compelling negotiation: creating leverage so the occupying power sees compromise as preferable to continued conflict.

3) Asymmetry and “making occupation costly”

Core claim: Colonized people often face extreme power imbalance. Proponents argue that irregular armed resistance can offset conventional military disadvantage by increasing the ongoing cost of control.

  • Eroding the occupier’s will: sustained costs (economic, political, reputational, military) can weaken domestic support for occupation.
  • Constraining operations: forcing the occupier to divert resources to security, reducing capacity to expand control.

Supposed benefits:

  • Restoring collective morale: replacing fear and humiliation with a sense of participation and purpose.
  • Strengthening identity and solidarity: creating shared narratives of struggle that unify disparate groups.

5) Signaling resolve and credibility

Core claim: If an occupier believes a population will not fight, it may expect compliance. Violent resistance is sometimes framed as a signal that domination will be contested indefinitely.

Supposed benefits:

  • Credible commitment: demonstrating that the population will bear costs for freedom can shift bargaining dynamics.
